name: The Serial Position Effect
statement: We remember the first and last items on a list best, the middle worst.
statementAccent: the first and last items on a list best
meaning: When people try to recall a list, they remember the items at the beginning and the end far better than those in the middle. Plotting recall accuracy against position gives a U-shaped curve — high at both ends, low and flat through the middle. The beginning advantage is called primacy, the ending advantage recency.
mechanism: Primacy arises because early items receive more rehearsal and processing time and so are transferred into long-term memory. Recency arises because the final items are still held in short-term memory when recall begins, so they are readily available. Middle items lose out on both counts: they are pushed out of short-term memory before enough rehearsal has moved them into long-term store. The two mechanisms map onto the classic model of separate short- and long-term memory systems.

examples.text: In free recall of word lists, people reliably remember the first and last words better than the middle ones, producing the characteristic bowed curve regardless of how long the list is.

Insert a brief distracting task between the list and recall — counting backward for half a minute — and the recency advantage disappears while primacy survives, the signature dissociation between the two memory stores.
The pattern extends informally to everyday memory, such as recalling the first and last people introduced at a gathering better than those in between.

variants.name: Primacy and recency effects
variants.text: The two halves of the curve — the early-item advantage from long-term memory and the late-item advantage from short-term memory — each with its own mechanism.

variants.name: The long-term recency effect
variants.text: The finding that a recency advantage can reappear even after a filled delay under some conditions, complicating the simple short-term-store account of recency.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most reliable findings in memory research and a cornerstone of the case for separate short- and long-term memory systems. Its clean experimental dissociation — a delay wiping out recency but not primacy — made it a classic demonstration in cognitive psychology, and it informs how lists, presentations, and messages are ordered.

working.lead: Place key items at the ends
working.text: put the most important points first or last, where they are best remembered, not buried in the middle.
treat the memory for the last few items as fragile, since a delay or distraction erases it.
reinforce the material in the middle of a list, which is most easily lost, through repetition or emphasis.

limits: The empirical effect is robust and highly replicated, but its interpretation is debated. The clean story that recency simply reflects short-term memory emptying is challenged by the long-term recency effect, in which recency reappears even after distractor-filled delays under certain conditions — which a pure short-term account does not predict, motivating alternative context-based and temporal-distinctiveness models. So the data, both the curve and the delay dissociation, are solid, while the mechanistic claim that recency is just short-term memory is contested.
misreadings: It is not that middle items cannot be remembered at all — they are recalled less well, not never. And the recency advantage is not permanent; a short delay or distracting task erases it, which is exactly what distinguishes it from the durable primacy advantage.
origin: The term traces to Hermann Ebbinghaus's nineteenth-century memory studies; the modern free-recall curve was characterised by Bennet Murdock in 1962, and Glanzer and Cunitz's 1966 delay experiment gave the key dissociation between the two memory stores.

sources.text: Ebbinghaus, H. (1913). “Memory: A contribution to experimental psychology.” — the English translation of Ebbinghaus's 1885 Über das Gedächtnis.
